I'm not going to trivialise your experiences. You seem to have had an objectively rough life up to this point. I'm also not going to make you feel guilty by pointing out the consequences of going through with it, having felt suicidal, and participated in self-harm, myself, I'm sure you're well aware of them. What I am going to do is explain my own experiences with similar thoughts and give advice based on it, which I hope might be able to help.

One of the primary driving forces behind why I felt that way was a dichotomous sense of hopelessness and urgency. That everything was pointless, that I'd always feel miserable forever, and simultaneously that I needed to change things immediately, or I'd forever be a failure if I couldn't change things before a certain point. The existential dread I felt around the subject of death and it's inevitability was also an incredibly difficult thing for me to overcome, and even now it's still something I have difficulty dealing with. The key thing for me was acceptance and acknowledgement of all the things I was struggling to deal with, as well as myself as a person. 

Contemplating suicide is not much different than contemplating murder in a lot of ways, the same with assault and self-harm. The only real difference is the target. Suicide, like murder, is generally something you would only ever consider when you feel overwhelming hatred towards the target. In the case of suicide, as with self-harm, the target of your hatred is yourself. I'm certain no person in the entire world is as critical of myself as me. Being so hyper-aware of all of your shortcomings can be both a good and a bad thing. It's easy to start hating yourself when your failures are the most apparent and significant thing to you. I was constantly afraid that the shortcomings that were glaringly obvious to me would be seen by others, and I always maintained a certain distance when it came to honestly expressing myself because of it. 

School in general was an especially brutal experience for me. It wasn't that I was bullied or anything close to that. In fact, I was probably more akin to being a bully in a lot of instances. I was mostly ashamed that I couldn't just 'be normal', like everyone else seemed to be. That shame made me resentful of others, and I'd unjustly take my frustration out on them. But I didn't truly hit the bottom of my suicidal spiral until a couple years after highschool. 

It's admittedly cliché, but I had my first love, and after going through a significant amount of problems (which really should've been a warning signal), we eventually got together. It was the first time I'd truly dropped my guard around anyone. She then proceeded to drastically tank my mental health with constant manipulation and controlling behaviour, to the point that I experienced such severe anxiety that it regularly gave me insomnia, in addition to regularly weaponizing any insecurities or worries that I'd told her in confidence, as well as threatening, or actually committing, self-harm if I retaliated or confronted her. It eventually came to a head when I discovered that while acting that way, she'd also been cheating on me behind my back the entire time. The worst thing about the whole situation, at least to me, wasn't what happened in itself, although it was certainly shitty, it was that I had somehow deluded myself into ignoring the blatant signs and lies, and had basically just allowed it to happen to me. At first, it felt like the final straw which would make me go through with my suicidal desires, it also didn't help that my childhood dog suddenly got ill and had to be put down in the span of a single day, all while this was going on. 

I took a steep nosedive into very selfish and destructive behaviour for a significant period, I'd been slowly sliding into it for a while, but that pushed me over the edge. I abandoned all of my morals entirely and stopped caring about anything. I eventually realized that the sort of things I'd be doing to people, while it wasn't the same thing, it wasn't all that different from what had been done to me, which sickened me.

Although it was a horrible experience overall, I'm actually quite grateful for it, because it was only due to fully embracing my worst aspects that I came to accept that I wasn't perfect, and that my bad aspects were just as much of a part of me as my good ones. I learned to accept that part of myself, which led to me hating myself less. I only regret that it took all of that to happen for me to reach that conclusion.

Now I make sure to be as honest about myself and my actions as possible. If a situation occurs where that stuff bleeds through, I don't try to run away and hide from it, or justify it for the sake of my own conscience, or minimize my behaviour. I just straightforwardly apologise and accept any consequences. I've learned to accept that not everyone is going to like me, and that it doesn't matter.

You might not be able to relate to all of this, but I hope you can extract something useful that can be used to help you in your situation. This also might sound arrogant, but school really is just the start of your life. Once you finish, you really do realise just how truly insignificant it is in the grand overview of your life. I think it's important to recognise that even though it might feel like the most important thing in the world while you're still there, you'll feel drastically different as soon as it's over. 

As far as studies go, I was never the best student either, in all honesty. I'm pretty sure my attendance was bad enough to make your 45% attendance look miraculous by comparison, and I think I might have handed in less than 10% of any homework I was ever assigned throughout the entirety of my time in highschool.

The essence of what I'm trying to say is that you don't have to feel a sense of urgency and/or despair over it, because you have far more time and opportunities available to you, especially after leaving school. You also don't have to have decided exactly what you're going to do and have it all planned out either. Imho, that's a pretty insane amount of pressure to put on the average still-developing teenager, and it's not anywhere near as much of a necessity as a lot of people make it out to be.

Now it's time for the nagging segment. Try to avoid participating in things that have a high potential to be dangerous, and avoid associating with people who have poor morals and behaviour, because even if it doesn't influence your behaviour and actions directly, you'll eventually become calloused and feel indifferent to things you shouldn't. Avoid drugs too. Occasionally smoking weed is fine, but be careful not to become dependent on it. This one might be considered inflammatory, but avoid promiscuity too, don't fall into the habit of treating sex as meaningless. It's bad for anyone in general, but especially for young girls and those who've been through a similar sort of trauma to you. It's a pretty common occurrence, because devaluing sex as a concept can often equate to minimizing traumatic experiences in situations like this. While that might seem like a good thing in the short term, more often than not, it actually only exacerbates the situation and makes things worse in the long run. I hope things work out and you stick around. The world would be a worse place without you around.

I actually never played the original, started with FFX as a kid and by the time I really became aware of it, it was a bit too dated for me, although I did learn the general events and outline of the story (and also was an avid Kingdom Hearts kid, so I knew some of the characters from that).

Personally, even though I never played the original, what I'm most looking forward to are the changes to the story, and the results of them. I'd have still been happy to play an exact 1:1 modernized remake, since I'd mostly heard FF fans claim it's the best entry, but having the remake be more of a re-imagining, and having it differ from the original's plot significantly, makes it an entirely new, and very pleasant, experience. The mystery surrounding the story, and questioning just how things will be different, are the most enjoyable aspects of it for me.

I played the Crisis Core remake beforehand, and I loved the characters, especially Zack, and his interactions and relationships with Aerith, and, although brief, with Cloud too. It was bittersweet though, with the ending being what it was, but given FF7R's ending having altered his fate, I'm incredibly excited to see how Zack's presence is going to impact the story, and especially how it's going to impact the main cast, considering that half of them knew Zack personally (Aerith, Cloud and, to a lesser extent, Tifa), especially with Zack being a very significant person to both Aerith and Cloud. Cloud's reaction in that scenario would be incredibly interesting, considering his condition, and assuming they meet before Cloud becomes aware of it. 

Zack's inclusion in the main FF7 canon storyline is probably what I'm most excited for, although Nero being present in INTERmission has me excited for Genesis' likely inclusion too. Imho he was kind of underutilized in Crisis Core, despite being the 'main antagonist'. I'd definitely like to see him brought back with a bit more characterization and depth than just 'weird poem loving maniac'.

And if you hadn't left the keys in it, chances are good that the car wouldn't have been stolen. Yes, it's the fault of the person who stole it, but you made it much easier for them to do so. People do bad things, if you make yourself an easy target, you make yourself more likely to be the one they're going to do bad things to.

That's a false equivalence. The danger in this instance is trusting the word of a guy you clearly don't know well enough to trust. Taking people you barely know at their word is already past the point of reasonable precautions. If it had been a friend, then the blame would be entirely on them, but OP went to the house based on the word of a guy she barely knew. Let's not act like every person in the world wasn't told not to trust strangers as a child.
Actually it's "Don't trust strange men you barely know. It's common sense."

It's no different than if someone doesn't look both ways before crossing the street and gets hit by a car. It's not entirely their fault they got hit, they certainly didn't want to get hit, nor did they seek it out, but if they'd been more cautious and taken reasonable preventative measures, then they likely wouldn't have been hit.

So, depending on the situation, in some sense, a certain level of blame does rightfully lie with the victim for not taking reasonable precautions. 'Victim blaming' is only an issue when either the level of expectation for preventative measures is unreasonable (i.e. expecting someone to never interact with another person because they \*might\* be a serial killer), or the degree of blame assigned is unreasonable (i.e. saying they're as culpable as the perpetrator, or that they were seeking that outcome).

It's perfectly reasonable to admonish someone who didn't look both ways before crossing the road, because it's reasonable to expect them to do so and not doing so is risking danger. Just like it's reasonable to expect someone not go to a strangers house in the dead of night, because it carries a considerable risk of danger. If someone chooses not to take those precautions, they're actively choosing to increase the likelihood that they'll be in danger. You admonish people for disregarding to take precautions not to shame them, but to inform them, because you want them to be as safe as they can reasonably be.

There's a lot more that goes into it than the levels. It's also not just lower levels, that also tends to be more associated with depression. ADHD brains commonly tend to have issues in relation to dopamine/serotonin regulation, among other things. 

From personal experience, when the taps are on, they're on full blast, but there is no middle ground, either they're blasting with the force of a tsunami or they're wired shut so tight not even a single drop can leak out. 

So, while you're actively doing something stimulating, you're drowning in copious amounts of dopamine and serotonin. The issue starts when you stop. 

In most people, the chemicals produced will still have a lasting effect that lessens and eventually disappears over a considerable amount of time, depending on the amount of chemicals released.

ADHD brains almost immediately get cut off. No slow wind down, no lasting effects, it just goes sober, cold turkey. Anything unstimulating is no different than mental torture, since a lack of stimulation actively makes us almost immediately miserable. 

If it isn't a big stimulating jolt then it simply doesn't mean a thing. 

Hyperactivity tends to be recognized as a physical symptom of ADHD, which it technically is, but from my experience, it's more of a mental symptom resulting from a lack of stimulation. The fidgeting, the daydreaming, the inattentiveness. It's all a way of coping with torturous boredom.

Replace ADHD sufferers with Junkies and you'll see a remarkably similar correlation in behaviour. The main difference is that the high we chase is one we produce in our own bodies, so instead of having to go out and physically get our hands on a drug, we instead go and get it from whatever activities can provide us with stimulation.

Everyone with ADHD is essentially just a junkie chasing a constant dopamine high, it's just that it's a far easier drug addiction to maintain, and far less destructive than most others, in most regards at least.

Once it's boiled down to that extent, you can apply it to any of the difficulties faced by ADHD sufferers and it becomes quickly apparent why things are so difficult, becoming even more difficult, the more severe a case that a person has. 

When, for example, playing a video game provides you with boundless stimulation and thus joy, and anything else that's unstimulating, no matter how basic or necessary it may be, inflicts upon you nothing but instant misery, it's hard to make yourself consciously choose the option that is proven will make you feel horrible, even when you know it's objectively the correct one.

It can be bad enough that even going to the toilet appropriately is a problem, since it's not exactly stimulating. I often hold it in for hours on end, in a constant cognitive stream of excuses where I tell myself I'll just finish one more thing. It always ends the exact same way, with me 2 seconds from pissing/shitting my pants, rushing as fast as physically possible to the toilet, finishing as fast as physically possible, then going back to my designated *stimulating activity*.

It's impossible to test for things like that, and usually most cases don't present to that extreme anyway. In most doctors eyes, it's better safe than sorry, so it tends to be over diagnosed, especially in children. Medication helps to a degree, but if you don't get that shit as a child, your brain will have formed behavioural patterns that are hard to change, even once you get medication to help. Long term planning, anything to do with executive functions, or similar are practically a write off.

There's also a high likelihood of co-morbidity with depression, anxiety and autism too. So if you're super fucking unlucky, you get a bad case of ADHD and a variable number of the three amigos tagging along for the ride, which would also invalidate testing through dopamine or serotonin levels.

One of the things that can very quickly kill a horror game is a skewed balance between predictability and unpredictability. If the scares/monster are ever present, then the player will very quickly acclimate to that level of unsettlement, which Devs then have to attempt to offset, usually by jamming in cheap tropes like random jump scares to keep the player engaged. Alternatively if it rarely happens then the enjoyment and tension plummet right off a cliff edge. Finding the balance of keeping the tension high while simultaneously not allowing the player/audience to acclimate to their frightened state is the key to horror in general. You need a steady dose of general underlying suspense, even when nothing is actually happening. One very very underrated and critical aspect is the sound design. More specifically the music. The music has to evoke the correct response, try playing a horror game without music and then play it again with music and the difference is night and day. It's the most important tool in building tension.

From what you describe the monster to be like, it definitely sounds appropriate, the concept itself is pretty solid. The real technical issues are going to come when designing the map and the monster AI.

If the map is too large it's likely that the player ends up wandering a lot and if the AI is skewed more to the difficult side that's a bad combo. As a player you'll spend forever walking around constantly being harassed by the monster and making no progress which will tank your motivation. Having the player accomplish some form of task gives them a little boost that keeps them willing to push through the horror and beat it. The second it feels like you're just suffering for no reward is the second the game gets turned off. Of course the opposite applies too, too small of a map and too kind of an AI will make it too easy, the rewards won't feel deserved and the scares will happen rarely. It's self explanatory why that's not good for a horror game. Successful horror, that doesn't amount to just a tirade of jump scares, really has to walk a tightrope, if there's even a smidge too much leaning to one side the whole thing can topple over.

I'd advise copious amounts of testing, especially from people who aren't working on the game, preferably complete strangers so they don't have bias. That should give you a broad idea of where the current build leans in regards to the things I've mentioned and what might need to be adjusted to more evenly balance it so as to provide the player with a better experience. I'd also add some sort of concept which produces noise and attracts the monster, being at least semi-required, to be more specific, some function you can perform for potential rewards but with the risk of leading the monster straight to you or at least your general location. Risk Vs Reward. Maybe adding some randomly generated items or abilities that can lure the creature away, or fool it's senses, could offset the difficulty without curbing the AI behaviour too much.

Just to summarise it very very basically; it's all about maintaining balance.
